Cayman Islands Economy Recovers After Hurricane Disruption

Economic activity across the Cayman Islands is gradually returning to normal after Hurricane Iris battered the territory last week, causing widespread disruptions to businesses and infrastructure. The powerful Category 4 storm, packing sustained winds of 140 mph, made landfall on Grand Cayman before sweeping across the Sister Islands, leaving a trail of property damage and power outages.

Among the companies affected was Nexteer Automotive Group Ltd, which temporarily suspended operations at its logistics facility near George Town due to flooding and supply chain interruptions. "We are relieved to report that our site sustained only minor structural damage, and all staff are safe," said Maria Forbes, Nexteer's Cayman operations manager. "Our facility resumed full operations on Monday, following extensive cleanup and restoration efforts." The company expects to fulfill delayed orders within the next week.

The storm's impact was felt across the archipelago, with local authorities estimating that more than 60% of businesses experienced at least one day of closure. According to the Cayman Chamber of Commerce, early estimates put direct economic losses at US$85 million, though this figure is expected to rise as assessments continue. Tourism, retail, and financial services were among the hardest-hit sectors.

"We've seen a remarkable community response," said Premier Angela McLaughlin in a press briefing. "The coordinated efforts of emergency services and business leaders enabled a swift reopening of most commercial activity." The government has pledged emergency grants and low-interest loans to affected small businesses.

Analysts at Caribbean Economic Insights said the Cayman Islands’ robust disaster preparedness and insurance coverage helped mitigate longer-term economic fallout. "While the hurricane caused significant disruption, rapid restoration of power and transport links has enabled a faster-than-expected recovery," said CEI economist Jonathan Clarke. "Barring further adverse weather, we expect the economy to rebound to pre-storm activity levels within the next quarter."
